item.title: “‘Empty is the world, empty is the world,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is it said that the world is empty?”…
item.description:
“‘Empty is the world, empty is the world,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is it said that the world is empty?” - “Ānanda, because the world is empty of self and anything belonging to self, therefore it is said that the world is empty. And what, Ānanda, is empty of self and anything belonging to self? The eye, Ānanda, is empty of self and anything belonging to self. Forms are empty of self and anything belonging to self. Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact … that feeling is empty of self and anything belonging to self. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind … Phenomena … Mind-consciousness … Mind-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact … that feeling is empty of self and anything belonging to self. And because it is empty of self and anything belonging to self, Ānanda, it is said that the world is empty.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.85

item.title: “O good friends, here someone associates with sensual pleasures, associates with unwholesome states. After some time, that person hears the noble Dhamma, gives wise attention,…
item.description:
“O good friends, here someone associates with sensual pleasures, associates with unwholesome states. After some time, that person hears the noble Dhamma, gives wise attention, and attains the true Dhamma and the Dhamma in accordance. And having heard the noble Dhamma, given wise attention, and attained the true Dhamma and the Dhamma in accordance, that person lives without associating with sensual pleasures, without associating with unwholesome states. By living without associating with sensual pleasures, without associating with unwholesome states, ease arises, and more than ease, gladness arises. O good friends, just as from comfort joy is born, so too, O good friends, by living without associating with sensual pleasures, without associating with unwholesome states, ease arises, and more than ease, gladness arises. O good friends, that is the first short path leading to ease, realized by the Blessed One, the Wise One, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

From: Dīgha Nikāya 18 – Janavasabhasutta

item.title: “Therefore, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline. Monks,…
item.description:
“Therefore, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline. Monks, just as near a village or small town there is a large sala-tree forest overgrown with trumpet-flower creepers. Then a man comes who desires the welfare of that forest, its benefit, its security from bondage. He cuts down the crooked, weak branches, throws them out, and cleans the forest inside. He properly cares for the straight, well-grown sala saplings. Monks, after some time, that forest becomes grown, prosperous, and increased. So too, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 21 – Kakacūpamasutta

item.title: “Monks, just as in a dense forest there is a large deep lake, and a great herd of deer lives near one side. Then a…
item.description:
“Monks, just as in a dense forest there is a large deep lake, and a great herd of deer lives near one side. Then a man comes who does not desire their welfare, does not desire their benefit, does not desire their security from bondage. He closes off the safe, secure path leading to happiness and opens a dangerous path, sets a male decoy and a female decoy. Monks, then that great herd of deer will later fall into bondage and decline. Monks, then a man comes who desires their welfare, desires their benefit, desires their security from bondage. He opens the safe, secure path, closes the dangerous path, removes the male decoy, and destroys the female decoy. Monks, then that great herd of deer will later increase, prosper, and become abundant.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 19 – Dvedhāvitakkasutta

item.title: “If anyone speaks of ‘a heap of the unwholesome,’ monks, he would speak rightly of the five hindrances. Indeed, the entire heap of the unwholesome,…
item.description:
“If anyone speaks of ‘a heap of the unwholesome,’ monks, he would speak rightly of the five hindrances. Indeed, the entire heap of the unwholesome, monks, is just the five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the hindrance of doubt. If anyone speaks of ‘a heap of the unwholesome,’ he would speak rightly of the five hindrances. Indeed, the entire heap of the unwholesome is just the five hindrances.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.52

item.title: “Venerable Gotama, I have a perplexity and doubt: ‘How should one understand the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama?’” - “Vaccha, your perplexity is enough, your…
item.description:
“Venerable Gotama, I have a perplexity and doubt: ‘How should one understand the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama?’” - “Vaccha, your perplexity is enough, your doubt is enough. It is on this point that perplexity and doubt have arisen. I declare the rebirth of one who has clinging, Vaccha, not of one who has no clinging. Just as, Vaccha, a fire burns when there is fuel, not when there is no fuel. So too, Vaccha, I declare rebirth for one who has clinging, not for one who has no clinging.” - “Venerable Gotama, when the wind blows a fire far away, what does Venerable Gotama declare as the fuel for that fire?” - “Vaccha, when the wind blows a fire far away, I say that the wind is its fuel. At that time, Vaccha, the wind is the fuel (upādāna).” - “Venerable Gotama, when a being gives up this body and is reborn in another body, what does Venerable Gotama declare as the fuel for that being?” - “Vaccha, when a being gives up this body and is reborn in another body, I declare that at that time craving (taṇhā) is the fuel (upādāna).”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 44.9

item.title: - What gives birth to a person? What always runs about? What undergoes rebirth? Because of what is there no liberation? - Craving gives birth…
item.description:
- What gives birth to a person?
What always runs about?
What undergoes rebirth?
Because of what is there no liberation?
- Craving gives birth to a person,
The mind itself always runs about,
Beings undergo rebirth,
Because of suffering, there is no liberation.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.56

item.title: - Who ages, who does not age? What is called the wrong path? What is an obstacle to the Dhamma? What destroys day and night?…
item.description:
- Who ages, who does not age?
What is called the wrong path?
What is an obstacle to the Dhamma?
What destroys day and night?
What defiles the holy life?
What is a bath without water?
How many openings in the world
Upon which the mind does not dwell?
I have come to ask the Blessed One —
Please tell me the answers!
- Form in beings ages,
The name-nature does not age,
Greed is called the wrong path,
Craving is an obstacle to the Dhamma.
Aging destroys day and night,
Women defile the holy life —
Ensnared in this defilement
Are all beings.
Austerities and the holy life
Are a bath without water.
There are six openings in the world
Upon which the mind does not dwell:
Laziness and heedlessness,
Lethargy and lack of self-control,
Drowsiness and sloth —
These six openings should be
Completely abandoned.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.76

item.title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins in the past … in the future … in the present who regard whatever in the world is agreeable and…
item.description:
“Monks, those ascetics or brahmins in the past … in the future … in the present who regard whatever in the world is agreeable and enticing as permanent, as happiness, as healthy, as safe, as self — they increase craving. Those who increase craving, increase attachment. Those who increase attachment, increase suffering. Those who increase suffering are not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that they are not freed from suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.66

item.title: “Monks, I do not see any other fetter by which beings, fettered, wander and transmigrate for a long time as this fetter of craving. Monks,…
item.description:
“Monks, I do not see any other fetter by which beings, fettered, wander and transmigrate for a long time as this fetter of craving. Monks, fettered by the fetter of craving, beings wander and transmigrate for a long time.

One with craving as companion
Wanders on for a long time.
Neither here nor there beyond such becoming
Can they cross the wandering.

Knowing this peril — that craving
Is the origin of suffering —
Free from craving, without clinging,
Mindful, the monk lives the homeless life.”

From: Itivuttaka 15
